warmup.q: The company tries a store that keeps each shop's sign-up record exactly as the program sends it, and checks nothing. Two years in, the team splits the shop's name into two fields, legalName and tradingName, for new shops only. Where does the knowledge of what a shop record looks like live now?
options: Nowhere: a store that checks nothing has no rules about shape
In the code that reads shop records, which has to handle both shapes
In the store, which rewrote the old records when the first new one arrived
In a list of field names the store built from the records it has seen
warmup.why: The store kept each record exactly as it was written, so old shops still have name and new ones have the two new fields. Something still has to know that, and with no checks in the store, it's every piece of code that reads shop records. The second section calls this schema-on-read. The first option is the tempting one: the rules didn't disappear, they moved. No store rewrites old records on its own, and a store only builds lookup lists for the fields you name.

sections.h: Tables make three things hard: changing shape, keeping data together, growing past one machine
sections.html:
Let's start with what the SQL track built. A table holds rows, and every row has the same named, typed columns: merchant_id is a whole number, name is text. You ask for data in SQL, saying what you want, and the database works out how to get it. Edgar Codd, a researcher at IBM, proposed this relational model in 1970.

So why store data any other way? Because tables make three things hard.

The first is changing shape. Every row has the same columns, so a new field means a migration, a script that changes the table, like the numbered ones in SQL from the JVM. In PostgreSQL, ALTER TABLE merchants ADD COLUMN vat_id text is quick: it only updates the catalog, the database's own list of tables and columns. But splitting name into legal_name and trading_name is an UPDATE that rewrites every row, and changing a column's type usually copies the whole table. Forms that change every few months become a migration every few months, or one wide table with a column for every country's fields, mostly NULL (empty).

The second is keeping things together. The payment screen shows a payment, the fraud checks run on it (tests for signs of a stolen card), the moment its money moved, and any refunds. Designing a schema: normalization and constraints taught us to store each fact once, in its own table. That's four tables, so the screen costs four lookups or a join, the SQL step that matches rows from several tables. Stored as one record, the screen is one read of one place. Keeping data that is read together in one place is called locality.

The third is growing past one machine. Say the machine handles 8,000 new payments a second at 70% busy, and the sale day needs 25,000. A bigger machine, called scaling up, is the right first answer for most apps. But there is a biggest machine, and when it breaks, every payment waits while a standby copy takes over.

The other answer is to split the data over many machines, each holding one part. That's scaling out, and each part is a partition (some products say shard). It brings three new jobs. Every read and write must first find the machine that holds its key, the value it's looked up by. Each key needs copies on other machines, called replicas, so one dead machine doesn't take its data offline. And a join, or a transfer between accounts on two machines, needs a round trip over the network, a message there and an answer back. That's about 0.5 ms inside one data centre, and about 70 ms between distant cities.

Stores that don't keep data in tables are often called NoSQL. Every family in this track gives up something tables have, usually joins, transactions across many rows or a checked shape, to make one of these three cheap. (A transaction is a group of changes that all happen or none do.) That's the picture for the whole track.

Two research papers started it. Bigtable is a storage system Google built for its own products, such as Google Earth and the index behind web search, described in 2006. It keeps every key in sorted order and cuts the sorted list into ranges, one server per range. Dynamo is a store Amazon built so the shopping carts in its online shop kept working while machines failed, described in 2007. It hashes each key, turning it into a number that picks a spot on a ring of machines, and keeps copies on several of them. The figure shows both.

Next, we'll take a closer look at the first hard thing: what happens to a record's shape when the store stops checking it.

aside.title: Where does the name NoSQL come from?
aside.html: It started as a hashtag. In 2009, a meetup in San Francisco about free databases that weren't relational needed a short name to post under, and #NoSQL stuck. It was never a design or a standard, so the stores under the label share little apart from not being tables. Many of them now speak a language much like SQL, so people sometimes read the name as "not only SQL". This track groups stores by their data model instead: the shape they keep data in, and the questions that shape makes cheap.

sections.h: Schemaless stores: the schema moves into the code that reads
sections.html:
Every table has a schema: the description of its records, which columns they have and the type of each. PostgreSQL checks every row against it. Many stores outside SQL check nothing and keep whatever they're sent. They're often called schemaless, and the name is wrong. Some code still has to know that a shop has a name and a country. If the store doesn't check that, the code that reads the data assumes it.

So a schema can live in one of two places. Schema-on-write means the store checks each record when it's written, and refuses what doesn't fit. A table is schema-on-write: an INSERT that puts text into a bigint column fails. Schema-on-read means the store keeps whatever arrives, and each reader decides what it means. Programming languages show the same split. Kotlin refuses to compile val n: Int = "ten", while JavaScript runs the line, and the trouble shows up later, when something uses n.

The usual place to meet schema-on-read is a document store. It keeps each record as a document, a block of named fields written in JSON, the text format met in JSONB, upserts and MERGE:

{"_id": "M-0042", "name": "Northwind Bikes", "country": "FR"}

MongoDB, a popular document store, is this track's example, and with no rules set it takes any document. Take the name split from the warm-up. New shops arrive with legalName and tradingName, and the old ones stay as they are. The reading code handles both: use tradingName if it's there, else legalName, else the old name. No migration ran.

The price comes later. Every program that reads shops must know every shape the data has ever had. And a typo in an import job (a program that loads many records at once), Name with a capital N, is stored without a word. Months later it turns up as a blank on somebody's screen.

Schema-on-read wins when records really differ, like sign-up forms that vary by country. Schema-on-write wins when every record has the same structure, because then the store enforces it in one place. The line is blurring from both sides. MongoDB 9.0 added a validation level, constraint, that guarantees every document in a collection (MongoDB's word for a group of documents, like a table) passes its rules. And PostgreSQL keeps schema-on-read documents in jsonb columns.

The third hard thing, growing past one machine, is where the two papers come in. Next, we'll build Bigtable.

steps: Read SchemaOnReadDemo.kt. It reads four shop records from three years of sign-ups, each in a different shape, the way a document store with no rules accepts them. (Document comes from MongoDB's Java library and holds one document's fields.) The function displayName is the only place that knows the shapes.
Before you run it, predict the name it prints for each shop.
Run it from the labs folder with the command below. Then add a fifth record in a shape the reader doesn't know, such as {"_id": "M-0080", "shopName": "Kiosk 9"}, and run it again.

Merchant records from three years of onboarding. */ fun main() { val stored = listOf( """{"_id": "M-0042", "name": "Northwind Bikes", "country": "FR"}""", // first version """{"_id": "M-0051", "legalName": "Volt Electronics SARL", "tradingName": "Volt", "country": "FR"}""", // name split in two """{"_id": "M-0063", "legalName": "Kools GmbH", "country": "DE", "vatId": "DE811907980"}""", // German forms add a VAT id """{"_id": "M-0077", "Name": "Brightside Cafe", "country": "IE"}""", // an import job's typo ).map(Document::parse) // a document store accepts all four as they are // the schema lives here, in the reader: every shape the data has ever had fun displayName(d: Document): String = d.getString("tradingName") ?: d.getString("legalName") ?: d.getString("name") ?: "<no name>" for (d in stored) { println("%-7s %-28s fields=%s".format(d.getString("_id"), displayName(d), d.keys.drop(1))) } }

sections.h: Bigtable: keep the keys sorted, then cut them into ranges
sections.html:
Take one question, "show shop M-0042's payments from today", over 2 billion payments. Let's build a store for it, one version at a time.

Version 1 is a hash map, like Kotlin's HashMap: one step to the value stored under a key. But it keeps its keys in no useful order, so "every key that starts with M-0042" means visiting all 2 billion entries.

Version 2 keeps the keys sorted, like a TreeMap, in dictionary order: compare two keys character by character. Now design the key so the question becomes its start, its prefix. In M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701 the shop comes first, then the time, then the payment's id. All of M-0042's payments sit next to each other in time order, and one day is one unbroken run. The store jumps to the first key at or after M-0042#2026-11-07 and walks forward until a key stops matching. That walk is a range read, and its cost depends on how many rows it returns, not on the size of the table. Put the payment id first and the same question visits every row again. The row key decides which questions are cheap.

Version 3 spreads the sorted list over machines, like a filing cabinet in name order whose drawers each have their own clerk. Cut the list into pieces that follow the key order, about 100 to 200 MB each. Bigtable calls a piece a tablet, and each tablet server looks after many tablets. A range read touches one tablet, or two when it crosses a boundary. A tablet that grows too big is split in two. When a server dies, a coordinating server, the master, hands its tablets to others, which read the same files from Google's shared file system.

Version 4 gives the value some structure. With one block of bytes per key, changing a payment's status means rewriting the whole payment, and the old status is gone. So Bigtable finds a value by a row, a column and a time. The paper writes it in one line:

(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string

A column name has two parts, family:qualifier, such as pay:status or risk:score. You declare the families when you create the table. Qualifiers are free, and a row stores only the columns it wrote, so a missing column costs nothing, not even a NULL. That's what the paper means by sparse, and it's why a new kind of column needs no migration. A cell, one row's value in one column, keeps several versions, each under a timestamp that says when it was written, newest first.

One rule limits what you can build on top. Every read or write under one row key is atomic: it happens completely or not at all, and no reader sees half of it. Nothing is atomic across two rows.

How does a server keep the list sorted while thousands of new keys arrive a second? It never edits a file in place. It writes each change to the end of a log, so a crash loses nothing, and keeps recent changes sorted in memory. Now and then it writes them out as a new sorted file, and merges old files in the background. That design is called an LSM tree (log-structured merge tree). Cassandra, a free database first built at Facebook, uses it too, and the Storage engines track builds one.

Sorted ranges make "one shop's day" cheap. But each range lives on one server, and while a dead server's tablets move, nobody can write to them. For a shopping cart, Amazon decided that was too long. Next, we'll build Dynamo, which keeps writing through failures.

sections.h: Dynamo: hash keys onto a ring and keep writing through failures
sections.html:
Amazon's requirement was blunt: "Add to Cart" must work even while servers and network links fail. Amazon also judged speed by the 99.9th percentile (Latency, percentiles and the tail), the time that 999 of every 1,000 requests beat. Even a rare stall when one server died was too slow. Dynamo calls each server a node. Let's build it one version at a time.

Version 1 puts each key on node number hash(key) mod S, where S is the number of nodes and mod gives the remainder after dividing. A hash function such as MD5, an old and widely used one, turns any key into a big number that looks random, so keys spread evenly. This breaks the day you add a node. Going from 4 nodes to 5 changes the remainder for 16 of every 20 hash values, so 80% of all keys must move at once.

Version 2 uses a ring. Lay every possible MD5 value around a circle, like the minutes on a clock face. Hash each node's name to place it on the circle, and hash each key the same way. A key belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise from it. Adding a node now only takes keys from the one node after it: with 5 equal nodes, about a fifth of the keys move instead of 80%. That trick is called consistent hashing. Picture clerks round a table, each keeping the folders numbered between them and the clerk before. A new clerk takes folders from one neighbour only.

Version 3 adds copies, because with one copy a dead node makes its keys unreachable. The first node clockwise, the coordinator, stores the key and sends it on to the next nodes clockwise, N nodes in all, usually 3. The paper calls them the key's preference list. Here the clerks stop being a good picture, since no clerk copies every folder for two neighbours.

Version 4 stops waiting for everyone. A write that waited for all 3 copies would be as slow as the slowest node. So Dynamo waits for W confirmations, called acks, and a read asks R nodes. When R + W is more than N, say 2 and 2 out of 3, every read reaches at least one node that has the latest write. These overlapping groups are called quorums.

Version 5 keeps writing when a node on the list is down. The write goes to the first N healthy nodes clockwise instead. The stand-in keeps the write with a hint, a note naming the real owner, and hands it over when the owner comes back. The paper calls this a sloppy quorum with hinted handoff. The stepper walks through versions 2 to 5.

The price shows up during a failure. Two writes to the same cart can land on different nodes, and the copies disagree. Dynamo doesn't pick a winner. It tags each version with a vector clock, a short list of counters, one per node, that shows whether one version was made after seeing the other. When neither has seen the other, a read returns both, and the cart's own code merges them. An added item is never lost, but, as the paper admits, a deleted item can come back.

One more trap hides in a name. DynamoDB is a database that Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon's business that rents out computers over the internet, runs for its customers. Its own 2022 paper says it shares most of a name with Dynamo and little of the design. A DynamoDB partition keeps copies in several availability zones, separate data centres in one area, and the copies elect one leader with a voting method called Multi-Paxos. Only the leader takes writes, so there are no vector clocks for your code to merge.

That's two ways to place data on many machines. Next, we'll look at what a store keeps inside a record, and which questions that makes cheap.

steps: Read PreferenceListDemo.kt. It puts six nodes on a ring at the MD5 hash of their names, then finds the three nodes that store each key.
Run it from the labs folder. Check one line by hand: from the key's percentage, walk clockwise through the ring printout and take the next three nodes. After 100%, carry on from 0%.
Before you read the last line, predict it. The coordinator of pay-81723 is down: which node stands in, and what does it keep?

code.title: PreferenceListDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l01.demo import java.math.BigInteger import java.security.MessageDigest // Dynamo hashes keys with MD5 onto a ring of 2^128 positions private val RING: BigInteger = BigInteger.ONE.shiftLeft(128) private fun md5(text: String): BigInteger = BigInteger(1, MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(text.toByteArray())) /** Where on the ring a hash sits, as a percentage of the way round. */ private fun percent(position: BigInteger): String = "%5.1f%%".format(position.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(1000)).divide(RING).toInt() / 10.0) /** Six nodes, one token each. Which nodes store a key, and what changes when one is down. */ fun main() { // each node takes the ring position of the hash of its name val nodes = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D", "node-E", "node-F") .map { it to md5(it) } .sortedBy { it.second } println("Ring (clockwise):") nodes.forEach { (name, token) -> println(" $name at ${percent(token)}") } // walk clockwise from the key's position; skip nodes that are down fun walk(key: String, down: Set<String> = emptySet()): List<String> { val position = md5(key) val start = nodes.indexOfFirst { it.second >= position }.let { if (it < 0) 0 else it } // wrap past 100% return (nodes.indices).map { nodes[(start + it) % nodes.size].first }.filter { it !in down } } val n = 3 for (key in listOf("pay-81723", "pay-81724", "ACCT#A-1001")) { println("$key hashes to ${percent(md5(key))}: stored on ${walk(key).take(n)}") } // one node is down: the write goes to the first N HEALTHY nodes (a sloppy quorum) val key = "pay-81723" val home = walk(key).take(n) val dead = home.first() val healthy = walk(key, down = setOf(dead)).take(n) val stranger = healthy.single { it !in home } println("$dead is down. $key goes to $healthy; $stranger keeps a hint for $dead") }

try.expect:
Ring (clockwise):
  node-A at   0.1%
  node-B at  21.2%
  node-D at  26.2%
  node-C at  42.2%
  node-F at  50.3%
  node-E at  94.9%
pay-81723 hashes to  79.0%: stored on [node-E, node-A, node-B]
pay-81724 hashes to   1.8%: stored on [node-B, node-D, node-C]
ACCT#A-1001 hashes to  48.6%: stored on [node-F, node-E, node-A]
node-E is down. pay-81723 goes to [node-A, node-B, node-D]; node-D keeps a hint for node-E

You get exactly these numbers, because MD5 gives the same hash on every computer. Two keys that differ by one digit land far apart, which spreads the work. Notice how uneven the nodes are: node-E owns 44.6% of the ring (everything from 50.3% to 94.9%) and node-D only 5%. Dynamo fixes that by giving each node many places on the ring, called virtual nodes. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys, in the Partitioning track, builds them.

sections.h: The families: what you store decides what you can ask
sections.html:
Bigtable and Dynamo decide where data lives. The data model, the shape a store keeps data in, decides which questions are cheap, and what the store can check for you.

Key-value is the simplest model: put(key, value) and get(key), with the value a closed box to the store. Dynamo is this model, and so is Redis, a store that keeps keys and values in memory. Two database researchers, Michael Stonebraker and Andy Pavlo, named the catch in a 2024 survey. Once a value has several fields, your code has to unpack it, the store can't find anything by those fields, and every join happens in your program. That's why DynamoDB grew into a store of items, records with named fields, with a sorted second part of the key (lessons 3 and 4).

Add a sorted second part to the key, let each row carry its own columns, and you get Bigtable's wide-column model. The name misleads. A column store keeps each column's values together on disk, so a report can read one column of a billion rows quickly. A wide-column store keeps each partition's rows together instead. Cassandra is this track's example (lesson 5).

Let the store see inside the value, a JSON document with nested fields and lists, and you get the document model. One document can hold a whole payment with its refunds inside it, so locality comes free (lesson 6). Store the connections themselves and you get the graph model: nodes, such as accounts and phones, joined by edges, such as "uses this phone". Neo4j, a database built for graphs, is the example (lessons 7 to 9). Search, time-series and vector stores are mostly one special index on top of these models.

Family You store You find it by In this track
Key-value a value, or an item of named fields its key DynamoDB, lessons 3 and 4
Wide-column sorted rows in partitions the partition key, then a slice Cassandra 5.0, lesson 5
Document JSON-like documents any field you index MongoDB 9.0, lesson 6
Graph nodes and their connections a start node, then a walk SQL and Neo4j, lessons 7 to 9
Search, time-series, vector text, readings over time, lists of numbers that describe meaning a word index, a time window, the closest matches the Storage engines track

Read each family as a model, a promise about which questions are cheap, not as a product. Most NoSQL stores now speak a language much like SQL, and PostgreSQL stores documents.

Two myths are worth dropping now. "NoSQL means no schema": every store here makes you declare a key, Cassandra tables have typed columns, and MongoDB 9.0 can hold every document to its rules. "NoSQL means no transactions": DynamoDB transactions cover up to 100 items, MongoDB has transactions across documents, and Cassandra 5.0 has lightweight ones inside one partition.

Tables still win when the questions aren't known in advance, when reports need joins, and when a rule spans many rows, like an account book whose two sides must balance.

Every family here makes you decide the questions before you choose the key. Next, we'll build the habit of writing them down first.

try.title: Sort five payment needs into families
steps: For each need below, write down the family you'd reach for first, and the key you'd look things up by. Commit to an answer before you open the expected result.

(a) Before storing a payment, check whether its idempotency key, a code the card reader sends so a repeated request can be spotted, has been seen before: in under 5 ms, 20,000 times a second. (b) Store shop sign-up forms whose fields differ by country and change every few months. (c) Find accounts that share a phone or a device with an account known to belong to a fraudster, up to three steps away. (d) Keep every card payment for 13 months and show one card's last 50, newest first. (e) Find the shop whose name someone typed as "Nrthwind Bikes".
try.expect: (a) Key-value: DynamoDB (or Redis), keyed by the idempotency key, one lookup per check. (b) Document: MongoDB, one document per sign-up, with a validation rule for the fields every country shares. (c) Graph: Neo4j, starting at the flagged account and walking "uses device" and "uses phone" connections. (d) Wide-column, or key-value with a sort key: partition by card, sort by time with the newest first, read 50 from the top. (e) Search: an index of the words in every shop's name that tolerates typos, such as OpenSearch, a free search engine. If you put (d) in PostgreSQL, you're not wrong at small volume. The question is when one machine stops keeping up with the writes.

refs.title: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around (SIGMOD Record, June 2024, PDF)

opening:
Picture the payments company from the SQL track, a year on. Its app records card payments for 40,000 shops in twelve countries, all in one PostgreSQL database on one machine. Shops in each country sign up with a different form, and the forms keep changing. At lunchtime the machine is 70% busy, and the forecast for the year's biggest sale day says three times as many card taps.

The obvious plan is a bigger machine, and for a while it works. Smart people stop there, because the SQL track made tables answer every question we asked. But machines come in a biggest size, and tables have two more habits that hurt as an app grows.

The last SQL lesson, SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations, ended by asking whether tables are the right shape at all. In this lesson, we'll find the three things tables make hard, build the two designs Google and Amazon published around them, and sort today's stores into families. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payments company whose one database couldn't take three times the card taps, and whose sign-up forms kept changing shape. A bigger machine comes first. After that, each family we met trades something tables give for free to split the data over many machines, or to keep a record's parts together.

Open your phone's contacts. They're sorted by name, so everyone called Kim is one jump and a short read away, while everyone in Lyon means reading them all. That's Bigtable's rule in your pocket.

Next, we'll write the questions down before choosing a key, and find out why a store spread over 40 machines refuses a question its key can't answer.

compare.title: One payment as a table row and as Bigtable cells

a.label: Table row
a.title: PostgreSQL
a.html: -- the schema fixes the columns for every row CREATE TABLE payment ( payment_id text PRIMARY KEY, merchant_id text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL, amount_minor bigint NOT NULL, risk_score numeric(4,2) -- NULL for most rows ); INSERT INTO payment VALUES ('pay-81701', 'M-0042', 'CAPTURED', 18000, NULL); UPDATE payment SET status = 'SETTLED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81701'; -- the old status is gone unless you keep a history table

b.label: Bigtable cells
b.title: row key, column, timestamp: value
b.html:
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:amount  t=100  18000
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:status  t=300  SETTLED
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:status  t=200  CAPTURED

# no risk:score cell at all: nothing stored, not even a NULL
# the update added a version; reads see t=300 first
# only the row key is indexed; there is no WHERE status = ?

compare.note: The table row has a fixed set of typed columns, keeps one current value in each, and lets you search on any column. The Bigtable row has whatever columns it wrote, keeps several timestamped versions of each cell, and can only be found by its row key or a range of row keys. That's why the row key carries the shop and the time: in Bigtable, the key is the question.

worked.title: Design a row key for "a shop's latest payments"

steps.say: Write the question down first: show shop M-0042's 50 most recent payments. A Bigtable-style store does two cheap things: get one row, and read a range of rows in key order. So the answer has to be one range.
steps.code: access pattern: merchant = M-0042, newest first, stop after 50

steps.say: First try: the payment id as the row key. Each payment gets a unique key, but one shop's payments are scattered across the whole list, so the question becomes a read of the whole table.
steps.code:
pay-81655  pay-81690  pay-81701  pay-81712  pay-81720 ...
# M-0042's rows are mixed in with every other merchant's

steps.say: Second try: shop, then time, then payment id. Now one prefix read covers exactly M-0042's payments. But they come out oldest first, so the newest 50 sit at the end of the range, and a forward read passes every older payment to reach them.
steps.code: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String) = "$merchantId#$at#$paymentId" // oldest first within the merchant

steps.say: Third try: store the time reversed. toEpochMilli() gives the time as milliseconds since 1970, and Long.MAX_VALUE minus that number gets smaller as time moves on, so the newest payment sorts first. Pad it to 19 digits so it compares correctly as text. A prefix read of M-0042# with a limit of 50 now stops after exactly 50 rows.
steps.code: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String { // newest first: bigger time, smaller number val reversed = Long.MAX_VALUE - at.toEpochMilli() return "$merchantId#${"%019d".format(reversed)}#$paymentId" }

steps.say: Check the price. Every new payment for M-0042 now lands at the start of the same range, which lives on one tablet. For a shop taking thousands of payments a second, that one server takes every write. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys, in the Partitioning track, spreads such a hot key over several ranges and merges them when you read.

lab.title: Build a tiny Bigtable: one sorted map of cells
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All seven fail with NotImplementedError for now. No Docker needed: this lab is plain Kotlin.
Write CellKey.compareTo: row in ascending order, then column ascending, then timestamp descending, so the newest version comes first. The first test passes.
Write put. Refuse a column whose family wasn't declared (familyOf is given), insert the cell, then delete every version of that cell beyond maxVersions.
Write versions. Start at CellKey(row, column, Long.MAX_VALUE) and walk forward while the row and the column still match. get is built on it, so its test passes too.
Write readRow and scan the same way: jump to the first possible key, walk forward, and stop at the first key that no longer matches. Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Why Long.MAX_VALUE? Timestamps sort in reverse, so the biggest timestamp makes the smallest key of a cell. CellKey(row, "", Long.MAX_VALUE) is the first possible key of a whole row, because "" sorts before every column name.
cells.tailMap(from, true) is a live view of the map from from to the end. Walk it with .entries.asSequence().takeWhile { ... } and you never touch the rest of the table.
In readRow, compare the row with ==. Row pay-10 starts with pay-1, and the test checks that you don't pick it up. In scan, startsWith is right, because there you want the prefix.
To drop old versions in put, collect the extra keys into a list first, then remove them. Removing entries while you walk a view of the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException.

drill.title: A newest-first row key from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write a Kotlin function rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String whose keys make a prefix read of "$merchantId#" return that shop's payments newest first. Then write one sentence on why the number must be padded. Compare with the answer.

answer.html: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String { // later time -> smaller number -> sorts first val reversed = Long.MAX_VALUE - at.toEpochMilli() // fixed width: as text, "10" sorts before "9", so every number needs the same length return "$merchantId#${"%019d".format(reversed)}#$paymentId" }

recap: Tables make three things hard: changing the shape of records, keeping data that is read together in one place (locality), and growing past one machine. Each NoSQL family gives up joins, transactions across many rows or a checked shape to make one of them cheap.
A schemaless store is schema-on-read: it keeps whatever arrives, and every reader carries the rules. Schema-on-write checks each record once, in the store. Use the first when records really differ.
Bigtable (2006) is one sparse map sorted by row key and cut into tablets. The row key decides where data lives and which questions are a cheap range read, and only a change inside one row is atomic.

Dynamo (2007) hashes keys onto a ring of equal nodes, copies each key to N nodes and keeps writing through failures with sloppy quorums and hints. DynamoDB shares the name and the hashing, but each partition has one elected leader.
Key-value, wide-column, document and graph are models, not products. Wide-column isn't a column store, and "no schema" and "no transactions" are both out of date.

The limit: every family makes some questions cheap by making others expensive, and you choose which when you choose the key. A question nobody planned for becomes a read of everything or a new copy of the data.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Let's move shop sign-ups to a document store. It doesn't check a schema, so we'll never have to think about schemas again." Explain what's right, what's wrong, and what you'd do.
explain.answer: The right part: sign-up forms differ by country and change every few months, and a document store can take each shop in the shape it arrives, with no migration and no table full of NULLs. The wrong part: the schema doesn't go away, it moves. A store that checks nothing is schema-on-read, so every program that reads shops must know every shape the data has ever had. And a typo from an import job is stored without complaint and shows up months later as a blank field. I'd use the document store for the forms, but put a validation rule on the fields every country shares (MongoDB 9.0's constraint level guarantees every stored document passes it). Then I'd keep one piece of reading code that turns every known shape into one Kotlin class, so the knowledge lives in one place.

deeper.html:
Dynamo's paper has a table that pairs each problem with the technique that solves it. It's the best one-page map of the ideas you'll meet later in the course:

Problem Technique Where you meet it again
Splitting the data Consistent hashing Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys
Writes that always go through Vector clocks, merged when you read Concurrent writes: last write wins, version vectors and CRDTs
Machines down for a while Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair
Machines gone for good Comparing copies with Merkle trees (trees of hashes) Leaderless replication: quorums, hinted handoff and read repair
Knowing which nodes are alive Gossip: nodes pass news to a few others, who pass it on Inside a Cassandra cluster: the token ring, gossip and failure detection

Bigtable leans on other Google systems, which its paper describes briefly. It keeps its commit log and its SSTable files in GFS, a file system shared by many machines, so a tablet server holds no data that would be lost with its disk. It uses Chubby, a lock service whose five copies agree using Paxos, to make sure only one master runs and to track which tablet servers are alive. When a tablet server dies, the master gives its tablets to other servers, which replay the commit log from GFS. That's a sharp contrast with Dynamo. Bigtable recovers by moving responsibility to another server, while Dynamo keeps several live copies and keeps writing.

Daniel Abadi's 2012 PACELC paper, which Consistency models: what a read may return opens properly, sorts these systems by two trade-offs. The first is what they give up when the network splits the machines into groups that can't talk. The second is what they trade between speed and up-to-date answers the rest of the time. By the paper's labels, Dynamo and Cassandra choose staying available and answering fast, while Bigtable and HBase, a free rebuild of Bigtable, choose up-to-date answers in both cases.

For the history behind the first section, read chapter 3 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (Kleppmann and Riccomini). It walks from Codd's relations through documents and graphs, and treats schema-on-read as a trade-off, not a feature. Stonebraker and Pavlo's 2024 survey is the sharper read. Section by section, it argues that each non-relational model either stayed a niche or grew back into SQL.
